Product design / revision 02 / simulated comparison

Lower the phone.
Let the feet do more.

A more compact biped with a landscape phone mount, shorter legs, a lower battery and broader feet. Modest body-angle feedback improves its balance. We retained all 14 actuated axes.

15%Less positive motor work

For the same first 10 cm of simulated travel: 5.23 → 4.44 J.

23 mmLower centre of mass

169 → 146 mm above the floor in the initial pose.

20%Lower torque-squared integral

For the same 10 cm task: 3.35 → 2.69 Nm²s, a motor-heating proxy.

These are improvements in simulated actuator effort, not measured battery savings. Both designs still use an early shuffling controller with substantial foot slip.

Left: original · Right: revised · actual MuJoCo state recordings · 12 N push for 160 ms in the push test

Hardware changes

The revised proportions.

FeatureOriginalRecommended V2
Phone orientationPortraitLandscape, nearer pelvis
Thigh / shin length80 / 80 mm70 / 70 mm
Each sole96 × 60 mm120 × 72 mm
Foot-centre spacing106 mm118 mm
Battery centreAt pelvis origin12 mm lower; narrower pack
Total assumed mass1.691 kg1.659 kg
Overall height367 mm277 mm
Body-angle feedbackNoneIdeal pitch/roll feedback to ankles

The larger feet add model mass; lighter, shorter link targets offset that increase. The revised pack proxy has approximately the same volume. Structural stiffness, real pack packaging, phone retention and full joint clearance still need CAD validation.

Same task / same distance

Measure work, not just time.

First 10 cmOriginalV2
Time from start6.03 s5.50 s
Positive motor work5.23 J4.44 J
Torque-squared integral3.35 Nm²s2.69 Nm²s

The one-second standing setup is excluded from effort totals. No stopping or final settling phase is included. Positive motor work integrates max(torque × joint speed, 0) across all actuators; it does not include electrical losses or credit regenerative braking.

Torque-squared integral compares heating tendency for unchanged motor/gear families. It is not electrical energy. Battery Wh and runtime need motor constants, winding resistance, gear efficiency, driver losses, phone and controller power.

Balance / honest boundaries

Better sideways. Forward recovery remains.

Six-second testOriginalV2
Movement, max tilt1.80°1.36°
Side push, max tilt106.7°, falls19.9°, no fall
Forward pushFalls at 2.236 sFalls at 2.266 s
Peak joint torque in movement0.76 Nm0.82 Nm

The same 12 N, 160 ms disturbance starts at t = 2 s. Body pitch/roll are read directly from the simulation, without sensor noise or latency. Larger feet and a lower body improve this test, but a recovery-step strategy is still needed for the forward push.

Peak torque rises about 8% during movement. Retain the assumed motor torque limits for now; lower total effort does not mean smaller peak-capacity motors.

Power-saving product behaviour

Spend energy when it helps.

  • Turn only the phone toward a person before rotating the whole body. Remain stationary when movement is unnecessary.
  • Use a deliberate parking mode. A mechanical support or verified locking mechanism could allow reduced drive current; this hardware is proposed, not simulated.
  • Balance the phone cradle around its tilt axis to reduce holding load. Validate every supported phone and case.
  • Throttle perception and radio activity when idle while maintaining local balance and fault monitoring. Measure whole-device draw before estimating runtime.

A small knee spring was explored in the parameter sweep but is not part of this recommendation. Smaller-amplitude steps also proved worse in work per metre in several tested cases. Neither change should be assumed to save energy automatically.

Validation performed

Promising, still a prototype.

  • Halving the timestep preserves the benefit: about 13.5% less work for the first 10 cm. The lateral-push test still does not fall.
  • The revised stepping test stays upright for 20 seconds. A 350 g phone case also stays upright in the six-second test.
  • The no-feedback hardware revision alone reduces six-second work per metre by approximately 11%; feedback provides an additional change.
  • Self-collision remains disabled; floor contact and friction are simulated. Motors remain ideal torque-limited position servos.

Sliding is substantial in both designs. The six-second summed contact slip-path metric is 0.36 m for the original and 0.39 m for V2, across both feet; it is not travel distance. A proper lift-and-place gait is the next development step.
